short: Decoder split (M06) and lip-reader text plus audio prompt (M07) are standard; WER gain comes from the lip reader, LRS3 WER level with LipVoicer, prosody leads confounded by the prompt.
position: RESOUND [@pham2025resound] changes the decoder (M06), splitting it into excitation and formant paths, and the use-time inputs (M07), adding lip-reader text and a 0.5 s audio prompt. Both are standard: vid2voc predicted F0, aperiodicity and spectral envelope from silent video for a source-filter vocoder [@michelsanti2020vocoder], and Let There Be Sound used pitch and energy predictors [@kim2024let], so the claim to be "the first study to incorporate source-filter theory into L2S synthesis" (§1; Appendix, M06) holds only as a label. The WER gain comes from the lip reader: without L2T and SRA, LRS3 WER rises from 20.06 to 27.49, level with Intelligible L2S at 27.69 (Tables 1, 3). With it, RESOUND is level with the best on LRS3 (20.06 against 21.04 for LipVoicer in its table, 21.4% in LipVoicer's paper [@yemini2024lipvoicer]) and trails LipVoicer on LRS2 (28.55 against 17.04). The prosody and similarity leads (MAEF0 49.52 against 81.63, SECS 0.777 against 0.591 for LipVoicer) pit a system prompted with audio (§3.3) against LipVoicer, given none. The SOTA claim (§5) has no reported repeated runs.
